concept.name: High-frequency trader
concept.definition: A high-frequency trader is a market participant using automated, algorithmic strategies characterized by very high-speed order generation, submission, and cancellation, extremely short position-holding periods, and infrastructure such as co-location of servers near exchange matching engines to minimize latency. HFT is a category of practice rather than a single statutorily defined registration type.
concept.intuition: An HFT firm is a sprinter among joggers: computers sitting next to the exchange react to price changes in microseconds, jumping in and out of tiny positions thousands of times a day.
concept.mechanics: HFT firms co-locate servers at the exchange's data center, consume direct market-data feeds, and run algorithms for market making, statistical arbitrage, and latency-sensitive strategies, typically ending the day flat. The CFTC glossary explicitly ties co-location — placing servers in close physical proximity to the matching engine — to facilitating high-frequency trading.
concept.failure_modes: HFT liquidity is fleeting: algorithms withdraw simultaneously in stress, contributing to flash events (e.g., the May 6, 2010 Flash Crash dynamics). Speed races also create arms-race costs and can make displayed depth unrepresentative of true resting interest.
concept.misconceptions: HFT is not a single strategy and not all HFT is predatory — much of it is ordinary electronic market making. Nor does speed alone guarantee profit; co-location and technology are costs, and many HFT strategies fail competitively.
concept.example: An HFT market-making algorithm posts and updates thousands of quotes per second in an equity index future, earns fractions of a tick per round turn, and flattens all positions before the close.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
citations.section: Co-location (defining infrastructure used to facilitate high-frequency trading)
